questions.topic: Period, frequency and amplitude of S.H.M.
questions.stem: In an experiment to determine the acceleration due to free fall, g, a student suspended a simple pendulum from a split cork held in a retort stand. For each effective length l (measured from the point of suspension to the centre of the bob) the bob was displaced through a small angle and released, and the time t for 20 complete oscillations was measured with a stopwatch. The readings were: l/cm: 30.0, 40.0, 50.0, 60.0, 70.0, 80.0; t/s: 22.1, 25.3, 28.4, 31.2, 33.5, 36.0. (a)(i) Calculate the period T for each length. [3 marks] (ii) Calculate T^2 for each length. [3 marks] (iii) A graph of T^2 (vertical axis) against l in metres (horizontal axis) gives a best-fit straight line which passes through the points (0.30 m, 1.21 s^2) and (0.80 m, 3.23 s^2). Determine the slope s of the line. [4 marks] (iv) Using the relation T = 2 pi sqrt(l/g), evaluate g. [3 marks] (v) Explain why the time for 20 oscillations, rather than one, was measured. [2 marks] (vi) State two precautions taken to ensure accurate results. [2 marks] (b)(i) Define simple harmonic motion. [2 marks] (ii) A simple pendulum of length 1.20 m is set swinging on the surface of the Moon where the acceleration due to gravity is 1.6 m s^-2. Calculate its period and its frequency. [4 marks] (iii) State two quantities on which the period of a simple pendulum does not depend. [2 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a)(i) T = t/20: 1.105, 1.265, 1.420, 1.560, 1.675, 1.800 s (deduct 1 mark for each wrong value)
3 marks: (a)(ii) T^2: 1.221, 1.600, 2.016, 2.434, 2.806, 3.240 s^2 (deduct 1 mark for each wrong value)
4 marks: (a)(iii) s = (3.23 - 1.21)/(0.80 - 0.30) = 4.04 s^2 m^-1 (2 marks for correct substitution, 1 for value, 1 for unit)
3 marks: (a)(iv) g = 4 pi^2/s = 39.48/4.04 = 9.77 m s^-2 (accept 9.6 to 10.0 m s^-2)
2 marks: (a)(v) Timing many oscillations reduces the effect of reaction-time error in starting/stopping the stopwatch; the period is found more accurately
2 marks: (a)(vi) Any two: small angle of displacement (less than about 10 degrees); bob swings in a vertical plane without spinning; counted oscillations from the centre of the swing / used a fiducial mark; length measured to the centre of the bob; avoided parallax when reading the metre rule; avoided draughts (1 mark each)
2 marks: (b)(i) Motion in which the acceleration of a body is directly proportional to its displacement from a fixed point (equilibrium position) and is always directed towards that point
4 marks: (b)(ii) T = 2 pi sqrt(1.20/1.6) = 2 pi x 0.866 = 5.44 s (2 marks); f = 1/T = 0.184 Hz (2 marks)
2 marks: (b)(iii) Any two: mass of the bob; material of the bob; amplitude (for small oscillations) (1 mark each)
questions.explanation: (a) T = t/20 gives 1.105, 1.265, 1.420, 1.560, 1.675, 1.800 s, so T^2 = 1.221, 1.600, 2.016, 2.434, 2.806, 3.240 s^2. Slope s = (3.23 - 1.21)/(0.80 - 0.30) = 4.04 s^2 m^-1. Since T^2 = (4 pi^2/g) l, g = 4 pi^2/s = 39.48/4.04 = 9.77 m s^-2 (about 9.8 m s^-2). Timing 20 oscillations spreads the reaction-time error over many swings. Precautions: small amplitude, swing in one vertical plane, measure length to the centre of the bob, avoid parallax and draughts. (b)(i) S.H.M. is motion in which acceleration is proportional to displacement from a fixed point and always directed towards it. (ii) T = 2 pi sqrt(1.20/1.6) = 5.44 s; f = 1/5.44 = 0.184 Hz. (iii) The period does not depend on the mass (or material) of the bob or on the amplitude (when small).

questions.topic: Acceleration due to gravity
questions.stem: A student used a simple pendulum to determine g and the radius of the bob without measuring the bob directly. The length l of the thread was measured from the point of suspension to the TOP of the bob. The time t for 20 oscillations was recorded for each length: l/cm: 40.0, 50.0, 60.0, 70.0, 80.0, 90.0; t/s: 25.9, 28.8, 31.4, 34.0, 36.2, 38.3. (a)(i) Calculate the period T for each length. [3 marks] (ii) Calculate T^2 for each length, correct to three decimal places. [3 marks] (iii) A graph of T^2 (vertical axis) against l in metres is a straight line which passes through (0.40 m, 1.676 s^2) and (0.90 m, 3.673 s^2). Calculate the slope s and the intercept c on the T^2 axis. [4 marks] (iv) Given that T^2 = (4 pi^2/g)(l + r), where r is the radius of the bob, evaluate g. [3 marks] (v) Use your values of s and c to determine r in centimetres. [3 marks] (vi) State two precautions taken to obtain reliable results. [2 marks] (b)(i) State the energy changes that take place as the bob moves from an extreme position to its lowest point. [2 marks] (ii) A bob of mass 0.050 kg is released from rest at a height of 5.0 cm above its lowest point. Neglecting air resistance, calculate its maximum speed. [g = 10 m s^-2] [3 marks] (iii) What is meant by damping of an oscillation? [2 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a)(i) T: 1.295, 1.440, 1.570, 1.700, 1.810, 1.915 s
3 marks: (a)(ii) T^2: 1.677, 2.074, 2.465, 2.890, 3.276, 3.667 s^2
4 marks: (a)(iii) s = (3.673 - 1.676)/(0.90 - 0.40) = 3.994 s^2 m^-1 (2 marks); c = 1.676 - 3.994 x 0.40 = 0.078 s^2 (2 marks)
3 marks: (a)(iv) s = 4 pi^2/g, so g = 39.48/3.994 = 9.88 m s^-2 (accept 9.6 to 10.0)
3 marks: (a)(v) c = (4 pi^2/g) r = s r, so r = c/s = 0.078/3.994 = 0.0196 m = 2.0 cm (accept 1.0 to 2.5 cm)
2 marks: (a)(vi) Any two: small amplitude; oscillations in one vertical plane; firm (rigid) support/split cork; avoided parallax on metre rule; avoided draughts; started counting from a fiducial mark (1 mark each)
2 marks: (b)(i) Gravitational potential energy is converted to kinetic energy (some lost as heat/sound against air resistance)
3 marks: (b)(ii) mgh = 1/2 mv^2, so v = sqrt(2gh) = sqrt(2 x 10 x 0.050) = 1.0 m s^-1
2 marks: (b)(iii) Damping is the gradual decrease in amplitude of an oscillation with time because energy is lost to the surroundings (e.g. against air resistance/friction)
questions.explanation: T = t/20 = 1.295, 1.440, 1.570, 1.700, 1.810, 1.915 s and T^2 = 1.677, 2.074, 2.465, 2.890, 3.276, 3.667 s^2. From the line, s = (3.673 - 1.676)/0.50 = 3.994 s^2 m^-1 and c = 0.078 s^2. Since T^2 = (4 pi^2/g) l + (4 pi^2/g) r, the slope gives g = 4 pi^2/s = 9.88 m s^-2, and c = s r gives r = c/s = 2.0 cm. (b)(i) P.E. changes to K.E. (ii) v = sqrt(2gh) = sqrt(2 x 10 x 0.05) = 1.0 m s^-1. (iii) Damping is the dying away of the amplitude because the system loses energy to its surroundings.

questions.topic: Elastic properties of solids
questions.stem: A spiral spring was hung from a rigid clamp with a pointer attached to its lower end moving over a vertical metre rule. With no load the pointer read 15.0 cm. Masses m were hung on the spring in turn and the pointer readings R recorded: m/g: 50, 100, 150, 200, 250, 300; R/cm: 17.0, 19.1, 20.9, 23.0, 25.1, 27.0. [g = 10 m s^-2] (a)(i) Calculate the load F (in newtons) and the extension e (in cm) for each mass. [4 marks] (ii) A graph of e in metres (vertical axis) against F gives a best-fit straight line through the origin passing through (0.5 N, 0.0201 m) and (3.0 N, 0.1202 m). Determine its slope. [4 marks] (iii) Hence calculate the spring constant k. [3 marks] (iv) Using your value of k, calculate the elastic potential energy stored in the spring when the load is 2.0 N. [3 marks] (v) State two precautions taken in the experiment. [2 marks] (b)(i) State Hooke's law. [2 marks] (ii) What is meant by the elastic limit of a material? [2 marks] (iii) A wire of length 2.0 m and cross-sectional area 1.0 x 10^-6 m^2 extends by 0.50 mm when a force of 50 N is applied. Calculate the Young modulus of the material of the wire. [5 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
4 marks: (a)(i) F/N: 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5, 3.0 (2 marks); e/cm: 2.0, 4.1, 5.9, 8.0, 10.1, 12.0 (2 marks)
4 marks: (a)(ii) slope = (0.1202 - 0.0201)/(3.0 - 0.5) = 0.0400 m N^-1
3 marks: (a)(iii) k = F/e = 1/slope = 1/0.0400 = 25.0 N m^-1 (accept 24 to 26 N m^-1)
3 marks: (a)(iv) e = F/k = 2.0/25.0 = 0.080 m; E = 1/2 F e = 1/2 x 2.0 x 0.080 = 0.080 J (about 0.08 J)
2 marks: (a)(v) Any two: pointer read at eye level to avoid parallax; spring allowed to come to rest before reading; elastic limit not exceeded (checked that pointer returns to zero reading on unloading); spring hung from rigid support (1 mark each)
2 marks: (b)(i) Provided the elastic limit is not exceeded, the extension of an elastic material is directly proportional to the applied force (load)
2 marks: (b)(ii) The maximum load (stress) a material can take and still return to its original length when the load is removed
5 marks: (b)(iii) Stress = 50/1.0 x 10^-6 = 5.0 x 10^7 N m^-2 (2 marks); strain = 0.50 x 10^-3/2.0 = 2.5 x 10^-4 (2 marks); E = stress/strain = 2.0 x 10^11 N m^-2 (1 mark)
questions.explanation: F = mg = 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5, 3.0 N; e = R - 15.0 = 2.0, 4.1, 5.9, 8.0, 10.1, 12.0 cm. Slope of e against F = (0.1202 - 0.0201)/(3.0 - 0.5) = 0.0400 m N^-1, so k = 1/slope = 25.0 N m^-1. At 2.0 N, e = 0.080 m and energy = 1/2 F e = 0.080 J. (b) Hooke's law: extension is proportional to load within the elastic limit. Elastic limit: the greatest load from which the material recovers fully. Young modulus = (50/1.0 x 10^-6)/(0.50 x 10^-3/2.0) = 5.0 x 10^7/2.5 x 10^-4 = 2.0 x 10^11 N m^-2.

questions.topic: Period, frequency and amplitude of S.H.M.
questions.stem: A light spiral spring was suspended from a rigid support and a mass m hung on its lower end. The mass was pulled down slightly and released so that it oscillated vertically. The time t for 20 complete oscillations was recorded for different masses: m/kg: 0.100, 0.150, 0.200, 0.250, 0.300, 0.350; t/s: 9.4, 11.1, 12.9, 14.4, 15.5, 16.9. (a)(i) Calculate the period T for each mass. [3 marks] (ii) Calculate T^2 for each mass. [3 marks] (iii) A graph of T^2 (vertical axis) against m is a straight line passing through (0.10 kg, 0.217 s^2) and (0.35 kg, 0.709 s^2). Calculate its slope s and its intercept c on the T^2 axis. [4 marks] (iv) The period is given by T = 2 pi sqrt((m + m0)/k), where k is the spring constant and m0 is a constant mass related to the mass of the spring. Use s to determine k. [3 marks] (v) Use s and c to determine m0. [3 marks] (vi) State two precautions taken in the experiment. [2 marks] (b)(i) Define the amplitude of an oscillation. [2 marks] (ii) A body performs simple harmonic motion of amplitude 0.050 m and period 0.40 s. Calculate its maximum speed. [3 marks] (iii) State the position at which the acceleration of a body performing S.H.M. is greatest. [2 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a)(i) T = t/20: 0.470, 0.555, 0.645, 0.720, 0.775, 0.845 s
3 marks: (a)(ii) T^2: 0.221, 0.308, 0.416, 0.518, 0.601, 0.714 s^2
4 marks: (a)(iii) s = (0.709 - 0.217)/(0.35 - 0.10) = 1.97 s^2 kg^-1 (2 marks); c = 0.020 s^2 (2 marks)
3 marks: (a)(iv) s = 4 pi^2/k, so k = 39.48/1.97 = 20.1 N m^-1 (accept 19 to 21)
3 marks: (a)(v) c = s m0, so m0 = c/s = 0.020/1.97 = 0.010 kg (accept 0.005 to 0.020 kg)
2 marks: (a)(vi) Any two: small amplitude; oscillations strictly vertical (no sideways swing); support rigid; timing started at a fiducial mark at the equilibrium position; avoided parallax on stopwatch/scale (1 mark each)
2 marks: (b)(i) The maximum displacement of the oscillating body from its equilibrium (rest) position
3 marks: (b)(ii) v max = omega A = (2 pi/T) A = (2 pi/0.40) x 0.050 = 0.785 m s^-1 (about 0.79 m s^-1)
2 marks: (b)(iii) At the extreme positions (maximum displacement), where the speed is zero
questions.explanation: T = t/20 = 0.470, 0.555, 0.645, 0.720, 0.775, 0.845 s; T^2 = 0.221, 0.308, 0.416, 0.518, 0.601, 0.714 s^2. Slope s = 1.97 s^2 kg^-1, intercept c = 0.020 s^2. Since T^2 = (4 pi^2/k) m + (4 pi^2/k) m0, k = 4 pi^2/s = 20.1 N m^-1 and m0 = c/s = 0.010 kg. (b) Amplitude is the maximum displacement from equilibrium. v max = 2 pi A/T = 2 pi x 0.050/0.40 = 0.785 m s^-1. Acceleration is greatest at the extreme positions.

questions.topic: Refraction of light at plane surfaces
questions.stem: A rectangular glass block was placed on a sheet of paper on a drawing board and its outline traced. A normal was drawn at a point on one face and incident rays at angles i to the normal were marked with two pins each. Viewing through the opposite face, two more pins were placed in line with the images of the first two, and the angle of refraction r inside the block was measured for each angle of incidence: i/degrees: 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70; r/degrees: 13.0, 19.5, 25.0, 30.0, 34.5, 38.0. (a)(i) Evaluate sin i for each angle, correct to three decimal places. [3 marks] (ii) Evaluate sin r for each angle, correct to three decimal places. [3 marks] (iii) A graph of sin i (vertical axis) against sin r gives a best-fit straight line through the origin, passing through (0.20, 0.300) and (0.60, 0.917). Determine its slope s. [4 marks] (iv) What physical quantity does s represent? [1 mark] (v) Using your value of s, calculate the speed of light in the glass. [c = 3.0 x 10^8 m s^-1] [3 marks] (vi) State two precautions taken to ensure accurate results. [2 marks] (b)(i) Define critical angle. [2 marks] (ii) Calculate the critical angle for glass of refractive index 1.50. [3 marks] (iii) State the two conditions necessary for total internal reflection to occur. [2 marks] (iv) Give two applications of total internal reflection. [2 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a)(i) sin i: 0.342, 0.500, 0.643, 0.766, 0.866, 0.940
3 marks: (a)(ii) sin r: 0.225, 0.334, 0.423, 0.500, 0.566, 0.616
4 marks: (a)(iii) s = (0.917 - 0.300)/(0.60 - 0.20) = 1.54 (no unit) (accept 1.48 to 1.56)
1 mark: (a)(iv) The refractive index of the glass
3 marks: (a)(v) v = c/n = 3.0 x 10^8/1.54 = 1.94 x 10^8 m s^-1
2 marks: (a)(vi) Any two: pins placed upright and well apart (at least 5 cm); viewed the bases of the pins/images to avoid parallax; block not moved during the experiment; sharp pencil used for fine lines (1 mark each)
2 marks: (b)(i) The angle of incidence in the denser medium for which the angle of refraction in the less dense medium is 90 degrees
3 marks: (b)(ii) sin C = 1/n = 1/1.50 = 0.667, so C = 41.8 degrees
2 marks: (b)(iii) Light must travel from an optically denser to a less dense medium; the angle of incidence must be greater than the critical angle
2 marks: (b)(iv) Any two: optical fibres; prism periscopes/binoculars; mirage; sparkling of diamond; reflecting prisms in cameras (1 mark each)
questions.explanation: sin i = 0.342, 0.500, 0.643, 0.766, 0.866, 0.940; sin r = 0.225, 0.334, 0.423, 0.500, 0.566, 0.616. Slope s = (0.917 - 0.300)/(0.60 - 0.20) = 1.54, which is the refractive index of glass (Snell's law: sin i/sin r = n). Speed of light in glass = 3.0 x 10^8/1.54 = 1.94 x 10^8 m s^-1. (b) The critical angle is the angle of incidence in the denser medium giving a 90 degree angle of refraction; for n = 1.50, sin C = 0.667 and C = 41.8 degrees. TIR needs light going from denser to less dense medium with incidence greater than C; uses include optical fibres and prism periscopes.

questions.topic: Refraction of light at plane surfaces
questions.stem: A pin O was placed at the bottom of a tall beaker. Water was poured in to a depth h. Looking vertically down, a search pin clamped outside the beaker was adjusted until it showed no parallax with the image of O. The vertical displacement d of the image (the distance from O up to the position of the search pin) was recorded for different depths: h/cm: 5.0, 8.0, 11.0, 14.0, 17.0, 20.0; d/cm: 1.3, 1.9, 2.7, 3.6, 4.1, 5.1. (a)(i) Calculate the apparent depth a = h - d for each reading. [3 marks] (ii) A graph of h (vertical axis) against a gives a best-fit line through the origin passing through (4.0 cm, 5.30 cm) and (15.0 cm, 20.01 cm). Determine its slope s. [4 marks] (iii) What does s represent? Give its value. [2 marks] (iv) Taking the accepted value as 1.33, calculate the percentage error in your result. [3 marks] (v) What is meant by 'no parallax' in this experiment? [2 marks] (vi) State two precautions taken. [2 marks] (b)(i) Explain why a swimming pool appears shallower than it really is. [2 marks] (ii) A fish is 2.0 m below the surface of a pond. Calculate its apparent depth when viewed vertically from above. [refractive index of water = 1.33] [3 marks] (iii) State the two laws of refraction. [2 marks] (iv) Calculate the speed of light in water. [c = 3.0 x 10^8 m s^-1] [2 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a)(i) a/cm: 3.7, 6.1, 8.3, 10.4, 12.9, 14.9
4 marks: (a)(ii) s = (20.01 - 5.30)/(15.0 - 4.0) = 1.34
2 marks: (a)(iii) s = real depth/apparent depth = refractive index of water = 1.34
3 marks: (a)(iv) % error = |1.34 - 1.33|/1.33 x 100 = 0.8%
2 marks: (a)(v) The search pin and the image of O coincide so that they do not appear to move relative to each other when the eye is moved sideways
2 marks: (a)(vi) Any two: viewed vertically from directly above; parallax removed carefully; beaker on a level surface; depth read with eye at the level of the water surface/bottom of meniscus (1 mark each)
2 marks: (b)(i) Light from the bottom is refracted away from the normal as it passes from water into air; the eye traces the rays back to an image above the true position of the bottom
3 marks: (b)(ii) apparent depth = real depth/n = 2.0/1.33 = 1.50 m
2 marks: (b)(iii) The incident ray, refracted ray and normal at the point of incidence all lie in the same plane; sin i/sin r is constant for a given pair of media (Snell's law)
2 marks: (b)(iv) v = c/n = 3.0 x 10^8/1.33 = 2.26 x 10^8 m s^-1
questions.explanation: a = h - d = 3.7, 6.1, 8.3, 10.4, 12.9, 14.9 cm. Slope s = (20.01 - 5.30)/(15.0 - 4.0) = 1.34; s = real/apparent depth = refractive index of water. Percentage error = 0.8%. No parallax means the search pin and image stay together as the eye moves. (b) The pool looks shallower because light bends away from the normal leaving the water. Apparent depth of fish = 2.0/1.33 = 1.50 m. Speed of light in water = 3.0 x 10^8/1.33 = 2.26 x 10^8 m s^-1.

questions.topic: Refraction of light at curved surfaces
questions.stem: A student used an illuminated object (cross-wire) and a screen to find the focal length of a converging lens. For each object distance u the screen was moved until a sharp image was obtained and the image distance v was measured: u/cm: 20.0, 25.0, 30.0, 35.0, 40.0, 45.0; v/cm: 60.4, 37.3, 30.1, 26.2, 24.1, 22.4. (a)(i) Calculate 1/u and 1/v (in cm^-1) for each pair, correct to four decimal places. [4 marks] (ii) Calculate f = uv/(u + v) for each pair and hence find the mean focal length. [5 marks] (iii) A graph of 1/v (vertical axis) against 1/u is a straight line. State the expected value of its slope and what its intercept on each axis represents. [3 marks] (iv) Calculate the power of the lens in dioptres using your mean focal length. [2 marks] (v) State two precautions taken in the experiment. [2 marks] (b)(i) Define the principal focus of a converging lens. [2 marks] (ii) An object is placed 10.0 cm from a converging lens of focal length 15.0 cm. Calculate the image distance and the linear magnification, and state two characteristics of the image. [5 marks] (iii) Name two optical instruments that use converging lenses. [2 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
4 marks: (a)(i) 1/u: 0.0500, 0.0400, 0.0333, 0.0286, 0.0250, 0.0222 (2 marks); 1/v: 0.0166, 0.0268, 0.0332, 0.0382, 0.0415, 0.0446 (2 marks)
5 marks: (a)(ii) f/cm: 15.02, 14.97, 15.02, 14.98, 15.04, 14.96 (4 marks); mean f = 15.0 cm (1 mark)
3 marks: (a)(iii) slope = -1 (1 mark); each intercept equals 1/f, about 0.067 cm^-1 (2 marks)
2 marks: (a)(iv) P = 1/f (in metres) = 1/0.150 = +6.7 D
2 marks: (a)(v) Any two: lens, object and screen aligned along the same principal axis; sharpest image located by moving screen to and fro; distances measured from the optical centre of the lens; experiment in a darkened room (1 mark each)
2 marks: (b)(i) The point on the principal axis to which rays parallel and close to the axis converge after refraction through the lens
5 marks: (b)(ii) 1/v = 1/f - 1/u = 1/15 - 1/10 = -1/30, so v = -30 cm (2 marks); m = |v|/u = 30/10 = 3 (1 mark); image virtual, erect, magnified, on same side as object (any two, 2 marks)
2 marks: (b)(iii) Any two: camera; slide/film projector; microscope; telescope; magnifying glass; spectacles for long sight (1 mark each)
questions.explanation: 1/u = 0.0500, 0.0400, 0.0333, 0.0286, 0.0250, 0.0222 cm^-1 and 1/v = 0.0166, 0.0268, 0.0332, 0.0382, 0.0415, 0.0446 cm^-1. f = uv/(u + v) gives 15.02, 14.97, 15.02, 14.98, 15.04, 14.96 cm, mean 15.0 cm. From 1/u + 1/v = 1/f, the graph of 1/v against 1/u has slope -1 and both intercepts equal 1/f. Power = 1/0.150 m = +6.7 D. (b) The principal focus is where rays parallel to the axis converge. For u = 10 cm, f = 15 cm: 1/v = 1/15 - 1/10 = -1/30, v = -30 cm (virtual), m = 3; the image is virtual, upright and magnified.

questions.topic: Reflection of light at curved surfaces
questions.stem: A concave mirror was mounted facing a lit object (a wire gauze in front of a bulb). For each object distance u, a screen was moved until a sharp real image was formed on it and the image distance v recorded: u/cm: 16.0, 18.0, 20.0, 24.0, 30.0, 36.0; v/cm: 48.3, 35.8, 30.1, 24.2, 19.9, 18.1. (a)(i) Calculate the magnification m = v/u for each pair, correct to two decimal places. [3 marks] (ii) A graph of m (vertical axis) against v gives a best-fit straight line passing through (18.0 cm, 0.50) and (48.0 cm, 3.00). Determine its slope s. [4 marks] (iii) Given that m = v/f - 1, use s to determine the focal length f of the mirror. [3 marks] (iv) What is the expected value of the intercept on the m axis? [2 marks] (v) Calculate the radius of curvature of the mirror. [2 marks] (vi) State two precautions taken. [2 marks] (b)(i) Define the principal focus of a concave mirror. [2 marks] (ii) State two uses of concave mirrors. [2 marks] (iii) An object is placed 6.0 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 12.0 cm. Calculate the image distance and the magnification. [4 marks] (iv) State one difference between a real image and a virtual image. [1 mark]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a)(i) m: 3.02, 1.99, 1.51, 1.01, 0.66, 0.50
4 marks: (a)(ii) s = (3.00 - 0.50)/(48.0 - 18.0) = 0.0833 cm^-1
3 marks: (a)(iii) s = 1/f, so f = 1/0.0833 = 12.0 cm (accept 11 to 13 cm)
2 marks: (a)(iv) -1 (when v = 0, m = -1)
2 marks: (a)(v) r = 2f = 24.0 cm
2 marks: (a)(vi) Any two: object, mirror and screen aligned on the principal axis; sharpest image found by moving screen to and fro; distances measured from the pole of the mirror; dark room used (1 mark each)
2 marks: (b)(i) The point on the principal axis to which rays parallel and close to the axis converge after reflection from the mirror
2 marks: (b)(ii) Any two: shaving/make-up mirror; dentist's mirror; reflector in torch/car headlamp/searchlight; solar concentrator; reflecting telescope (1 mark each)
4 marks: (b)(iii) 1/v = 1/f - 1/u = 1/12 - 1/6 = -1/12 (2 marks); v = -12 cm, i.e. virtual image 12 cm behind the mirror (1 mark); m = 12/6 = 2 (1 mark)
1 mark: (b)(iv) A real image can be formed on a screen (rays actually meet); a virtual image cannot (rays only appear to meet)
questions.explanation: m = v/u = 3.02, 1.99, 1.51, 1.01, 0.66, 0.50. Slope s = (3.00 - 0.50)/(48.0 - 18.0) = 0.0833 cm^-1, and since m = v/f - 1, f = 1/s = 12.0 cm; the m intercept should be -1. Radius of curvature r = 2f = 24.0 cm. (b) For u = 6.0 cm, f = 12 cm: 1/v = 1/12 - 1/6 = -1/12, so v = -12 cm (virtual, behind the mirror) and m = 2.

questions.topic: Refraction of light at plane surfaces
questions.stem: The outline ABC of an equilateral glass prism (refracting angle A = 60 degrees) was traced on paper. Rays were directed at face AB at different angles of incidence i using two pins, and the emergent ray from face AC was located with two more pins. The angle of emergence e was measured each time: i/degrees: 30, 35, 40, 45, 50, 55, 60, 65, 70; e/degrees: 77.0, 66.0, 58.5, 52.5, 47.0, 42.5, 39.0, 35.5, 33.0. (a)(i) Calculate the angle of deviation D = i + e - A for each reading. [4 marks] (ii) From your values, state the minimum deviation D_min and the angle of incidence at which it occurs. [2 marks] (iii) Describe the shape of a graph of D against i. [2 marks] (iv) Using n = sin((A + D_min)/2)/sin(A/2), calculate the refractive index of the glass. [5 marks] (v) What is the relationship between i and e at minimum deviation? [1 mark] (vi) State two precautions taken. [2 marks] (b)(i) What is meant by dispersion of white light? [2 marks] (ii) Which colour of white light is deviated most, and which least, by a glass prism? [2 marks] (iii) Explain why white light is dispersed by a prism. [2 marks] (iv) Calculate the speed of light in glass of refractive index 1.50. [c = 3.0 x 10^8 m s^-1] [3 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
4 marks: (a)(i) D/degrees: 47.0, 41.0, 38.5, 37.5, 37.0, 37.5, 39.0, 40.5, 43.0
2 marks: (a)(ii) D_min = 37.0 degrees, at i = 50 degrees
2 marks: (a)(iii) A smooth U-shaped curve: D falls to a minimum and then rises as i increases
5 marks: (a)(iv) n = sin((60 + 37.0)/2)/sin 30 = sin 48.50/0.500 (2 marks) = 0.749/0.500 (1 mark) = 1.50 (2 marks)
1 mark: (a)(v) i = e (the ray passes symmetrically through the prism)
2 marks: (a)(vi) Any two: pins upright and far apart; viewed bases of pins to avoid parallax; prism not moved; protractor read correctly at the normal; fine pencil lines (1 mark each)
2 marks: (b)(i) The separation of white light into its component colours (spectrum) when it passes through a prism
2 marks: (b)(ii) Violet is deviated most (1 mark); red is deviated least (1 mark)
2 marks: (b)(iii) Each colour travels at a different speed in glass, so glass has a different refractive index for each colour and each colour is refracted through a different angle
3 marks: (b)(iv) v = c/n = 3.0 x 10^8/1.50 = 2.0 x 10^8 m s^-1
questions.explanation: D = i + e - 60: 47.0, 41.0, 38.5, 37.5, 37.0, 37.5, 39.0, 40.5, 43.0 degrees. The smallest value is 37.0 degrees at i = 50 degrees; D against i is a U-shaped curve with this minimum. n = sin((60 + 37.0)/2)/sin 30 = sin 48.50/0.5 = 1.50. At minimum deviation i = e. (b) Dispersion is the splitting of white light into colours; violet is deviated most and red least because the refractive index of glass differs for each colour (each travels at a different speed). Speed in glass of n = 1.50 is 2.0 x 10^8 m s^-1.

questions.topic: Potential difference and electric current
questions.stem: A student set up a circuit consisting of an accumulator, a key, a rheostat, an ammeter and a resistor X in series, with a voltmeter connected across X. The rheostat was adjusted to give different currents I, and the corresponding p.d. V across X was read: I/A: 0.20, 0.30, 0.40, 0.50, 0.60, 0.70; V/V: 0.82, 1.17, 1.64, 2.00, 2.36, 2.83. (a)(i) Calculate V/I for each pair of readings. [3 marks] (ii) Find the mean of the values of V/I. [2 marks] (iii) A graph of V (vertical axis) against I gives a best-fit straight line through the origin passing through (0.20 A, 0.80 V) and (0.70 A, 2.80 V). Determine its slope. [4 marks] (iv) What does the line passing through the origin tell you about X? [2 marks] (v) Using the slope, calculate the power dissipated in X when the current is 0.50 A. [2 marks] (vi) State two precautions taken. [2 marks] (b)(i) State Ohm's law. [2 marks] (ii) A 6.0 ohm resistor and a 3.0 ohm resistor are connected in parallel, and the combination is in series with a 2.0 ohm resistor across a 12 V battery of negligible internal resistance. Calculate (I) the total resistance, (II) the current drawn from the battery, (III) the current in the 6.0 ohm resistor. [6 marks] (iii) Give two examples of non-ohmic conductors. [2 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a)(i) V/I in ohms: 4.10, 3.90, 4.10, 4.00, 3.93, 4.04
2 marks: (a)(ii) mean = 4.01 ohms
4 marks: (a)(iii) slope = (2.80 - 0.80)/(0.70 - 0.20) = 4.00 ohms (V A^-1)
2 marks: (a)(iv) V is directly proportional to I, so X obeys Ohm's law (its resistance is constant) at constant temperature
2 marks: (a)(v) P = I^2 R = 0.50^2 x 4.00 = 1.00 W
2 marks: (a)(vi) Any two: key opened between readings to prevent heating of X; meters read at eye level/avoid parallax; checked zero errors of meters; tight connections; ammeter in series, voltmeter in parallel with correct polarity (1 mark each)
2 marks: (b)(i) The current through a metallic conductor is directly proportional to the p.d. across its ends, provided the temperature and other physical conditions remain constant
6 marks: (b)(ii) (I) parallel: 6 x 3/(6 + 3) = 2.0 ohms; total = 2.0 + 2.0 = 4.0 ohms (2 marks) (II) I = 12/4.0 = 3.0 A (2 marks) (III) p.d. across parallel part = 3.0 x 2.0 = 6.0 V, current in 6.0 ohm = 6.0/6.0 = 1.0 A (2 marks)
2 marks: (b)(iii) Any two: filament lamp; semiconductor diode; thermistor; electrolytes/gas discharge tube (1 mark each)
questions.explanation: V/I = 4.10, 3.90, 4.10, 4.00, 3.93, 4.04 ohms, mean 4.01 ohms. Slope = (2.80 - 0.80)/(0.70 - 0.20) = 4.00 ohms = resistance of X. A straight line through the origin shows V proportional to I, so X is ohmic. P = I^2 R = 0.25 x 4.00 = 1.00 W. (b) Parallel 6 and 3 ohms = 2 ohms; total 4 ohms; current 3.0 A; p.d. across parallel part 6.0 V, so 1.0 A flows in the 6 ohm resistor.

questions.topic: Measurement of electric current, p.d., resistance, e.m.f. and internal resistance of a cell
questions.stem: A metre bridge was used to determine the resistance X of a coil. A standard resistor R was connected in the left-hand gap and X in the right-hand gap. A galvanometer connected to a jockey was used to find the balance point on the wire, a distance l from the left-hand end. The readings were: R/ohm: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6; l/cm: 25.1, 39.9, 50.2, 57.0, 62.6, 66.5. (a)(i) For each reading calculate (100 - l) and l/(100 - l), the latter correct to three decimal places. [4 marks] (ii) Using R/X = l/(100 - l), calculate X for each reading and hence the mean value of X. [5 marks] (iii) Explain how X could be obtained from a graph of R against l/(100 - l). [2 marks] (iv) State two precautions taken in the experiment. [2 marks] (v) Why is it best to choose R so that the balance point is near the middle of the wire? [2 marks] (b)(i) Define resistivity. [2 marks] (ii) The coil X is made from wire of length 1.0 m and diameter 0.50 mm. Using X = 3.0 ohms, calculate the resistivity of the material. [pi = 3.14] [4 marks] (iii) State the condition for a Wheatstone bridge to be balanced. [2 marks] (iv) Why is a galvanometer, rather than an ammeter, used to detect the balance point? [2 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
4 marks: (a)(i) (100 - l)/cm: 74.9, 60.1, 49.8, 43.0, 37.4, 33.5 (2 marks); l/(100 - l): 0.335, 0.664, 1.008, 1.326, 1.674, 1.985 (2 marks)
5 marks: (a)(ii) X = R(100 - l)/l: 2.98, 3.01, 2.98, 3.02, 2.99, 3.02 ohms (4 marks); mean X = 3.00 ohms (1 mark)
2 marks: (a)(iii) Since R = X [l/(100 - l)], the graph is a straight line through the origin whose slope equals X
2 marks: (a)(iv) Any two: jockey tapped lightly, not slid along the wire; key opened between readings to avoid heating; tight connections/clean terminals; protective resistor in series with galvanometer at first; balance point read without parallax (1 mark each)
2 marks: (a)(v) Errors in locating the balance point (and end-effects) then cause the smallest percentage error in l and (100 - l)
2 marks: (b)(i) Resistivity is the resistance of a conductor of unit length and unit cross-sectional area of the material (rho = RA/L); unit ohm metre
4 marks: (b)(ii) A = pi d^2/4 = 3.14 x (0.50 x 10^-3)^2/4 = 1.96 x 10^-7 m^2 (2 marks); rho = RA/L = 3.0 x 1.96 x 10^-7/1.0 = 5.9 x 10^-7 ohm m (2 marks)
2 marks: (b)(iii) No current flows through the galvanometer; the ratio of resistances in one pair of arms equals that in the other (P/Q = R/S)
2 marks: (b)(iv) A galvanometer is very sensitive and has a centre zero, so it detects very small currents in either direction
questions.explanation: (100 - l) = 74.9, 60.1, 49.8, 43.0, 37.4, 33.5 cm; l/(100 - l) = 0.335, 0.664, 1.008, 1.326, 1.674, 1.985. X = R(100 - l)/l = 2.98, 3.01, 2.98, 3.02, 2.99, 3.02 ohms, mean 3.00 ohms. A graph of R against l/(100 - l) is a straight line through the origin with slope X. (b) Resistivity rho = RA/L. A = 3.14 x (0.50 x 10^-3)^2/4 = 1.96 x 10^-7 m^2, so rho = 3.0 x 1.96 x 10^-7/1.0 = 5.9 x 10^-7 ohm m. At balance no current flows in the galvanometer, which is used because it detects tiny currents either way.

questions.topic: Measurement of electric current, p.d., resistance, e.m.f. and internal resistance of a cell
questions.stem: A potentiometer wire was connected to a driver accumulator. A dry cell E, with a resistance box R and a key connected across it, was used with a galvanometer and jockey to find balance lengths. With the key open the balance length was 75.0 cm. With the key closed, the balance length l was found for different values of R: R/ohm: 2, 3, 4, 5, 8, 10; l/cm: 50.1, 56.2, 60.1, 62.3, 66.8, 68.2. (a)(i) Calculate 1/R (to three decimal places) and 1/l (to four decimal places) for each reading. [4 marks] (ii) A graph of 1/l (vertical axis, in cm^-1) against 1/R (in ohm^-1) gives a best-fit line passing through (0.10, 0.0147) and (0.50, 0.0200). Determine its slope s and its intercept c on the 1/l axis. [5 marks] (iii) Given that 1/l = (r/l0)(1/R) + 1/l0, where r is the internal resistance of the cell and l0 is the open-circuit balance length, use s and c to find r. [3 marks] (iv) State two precautions taken. [2 marks] (v) Explain why a potentiometer measures the e.m.f. of a cell more accurately than a voltmeter. [2 marks] (b)(i) Define the e.m.f. of a cell. [2 marks] (ii) A cell of e.m.f. 1.5 V and internal resistance 0.50 ohm is connected to a 2.5 ohm resistor. Calculate the current, the terminal p.d. and the 'lost volts'. [5 marks] (iii) State two advantages of a potentiometer over a moving-coil voltmeter. [2 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
4 marks: (a)(i) 1/R: 0.500, 0.333, 0.250, 0.200, 0.125, 0.100 (2 marks); 1/l: 0.0200, 0.0178, 0.0166, 0.0161, 0.0150, 0.0147 cm^-1 (2 marks)
5 marks: (a)(ii) s = (0.0200 - 0.0147)/(0.50 - 0.10) = 0.0133 ohm cm^-1 (3 marks); c = 0.0147 - 0.0133 x 0.10 = 0.0134 cm^-1 (2 marks)
3 marks: (a)(iii) s/c = r, so r = 0.0133/0.0134 = 0.99 ohm (accept 0.8 to 1.2 ohm)
2 marks: (a)(iv) Any two: jockey tapped, not dragged, on the wire; key closed only when taking readings; driver cell e.m.f. greater than that of E; positive terminals connected to the same end of the wire; tight connections (1 mark each)
2 marks: (a)(v) At balance no current is drawn from the cell, so there is no p.d. lost across its internal resistance; a voltmeter draws current and reads the terminal p.d.
2 marks: (b)(i) The e.m.f. is the energy converted to electrical energy per unit charge driven round a complete circuit, i.e. the p.d. across the cell on open circuit
5 marks: (b)(ii) I = E/(R + r) = 1.5/3.0 = 0.50 A (2 marks); terminal p.d. = IR = 0.50 x 2.5 = 1.25 V (2 marks); lost volts = Ir = 0.25 V (1 mark)
2 marks: (b)(iii) Any two: draws no current at balance (measures true e.m.f.); more accurate/sensitive (long scale); can be used to compare e.m.f.s and measure small p.d.s (1 mark each)
questions.explanation: 1/R = 0.500, 0.333, 0.250, 0.200, 0.125, 0.100 ohm^-1; 1/l = 0.0200, 0.0178, 0.0166, 0.0161, 0.0150, 0.0147 cm^-1. Slope s = 0.0133, intercept c = 0.0134 cm^-1 (so l0 = 1/c = 74.8 cm, close to the measured 75.0 cm). Since s = r/l0 and c = 1/l0, r = s/c = 0.99 ohm. (b) E.m.f. is the open-circuit p.d. (energy per coulomb). I = 1.5/(2.5 + 0.5) = 0.50 A; terminal p.d. = 1.25 V; lost volts = 0.25 V.

questions.topic: Measurement of electric current, p.d., resistance, e.m.f. and internal resistance of a cell
questions.stem: Two dry cells in series (battery B) were connected in series with an ammeter, a key and a resistance box R. A high-resistance voltmeter was connected across the terminals of B. For different values of R, the current I and terminal p.d. V were recorded: R/ohm: 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 10; I/A: 0.94, 0.71, 0.58, 0.42, 0.33, 0.27; V/V: 1.90, 2.12, 2.32, 2.50, 2.60, 2.70. (a)(i) Calculate V/I for each reading, correct to one decimal place, and comment on your values. [3 marks] (ii) A graph of V (vertical axis) against I is a straight line passing through (0.30 A, 2.65 V) and (0.90 A, 1.93 V). Determine its slope and its intercept on the V axis. [5 marks] (iii) Given that V = E - Ir, deduce the e.m.f. E and the internal resistance r of B. [4 marks] (iv) State two precautions taken. [2 marks] (v) Why should the key be opened between readings? [2 marks] (b)(i) Distinguish between the e.m.f. of a cell and its terminal p.d. [2 marks] (ii) Three cells, each of e.m.f. 1.5 V and internal resistance 0.50 ohm, are connected in series to an external resistor of 3.5 ohms. Calculate the current in the circuit and the terminal p.d. of the battery. [5 marks] (iii) State one advantage of connecting cells in parallel. [2 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a)(i) V/I/ohm: 2.0, 3.0, 4.0, 6.0, 7.9, 10.0 (2 marks); values agree (approximately) with the resistance-box settings R, since V is the p.d. across R (1 mark)
5 marks: (a)(ii) slope = (1.93 - 2.65)/(0.90 - 0.30) = -1.20 V A^-1 (3 marks); intercept = 2.65 - (-1.20)(0.30) = 3.01 V (2 marks)
4 marks: (a)(iii) E = intercept = 3.01 V (accept 2.9 to 3.1 V) (2 marks); r = -slope = 1.20 ohm (accept 1.0 to 1.4 ohm) (2 marks)
2 marks: (a)(iv) Any two: meters read at eye level/avoid parallax; zero errors checked; tight connections; key opened between readings (1 mark each)
2 marks: (a)(v) To prevent the cells from running down (polarising) and the resistors from heating, which would change E, r and R
2 marks: (b)(i) E.m.f. is the p.d. across the cell when it supplies no current (open circuit); terminal p.d. is the p.d. across the cell when it is supplying current, and is less than e.m.f. by Ir
5 marks: (b)(ii) total e.m.f. = 4.5 V; total internal resistance = 1.5 ohm (1 mark); I = 4.5/(3.5 + 1.5) = 0.90 A (2 marks); terminal p.d. = IR = 0.90 x 3.5 = 3.15 V (2 marks)
2 marks: (b)(iii) The current is shared between cells so they last longer / the combined internal resistance is reduced
questions.explanation: V/I = 2.0, 3.0, 4.0, 6.0, 7.9, 10.0 ohm, approximately equal to R. Slope = -1.20 V A^-1 and intercept = 3.01 V. From V = E - Ir, E = intercept = 3.01 V and r = -slope = 1.20 ohm. (b) E.m.f. is the open-circuit p.d.; terminal p.d. = E - Ir when current flows. Three cells: E = 4.5 V, r = 1.5 ohm, I = 4.5/5.0 = 0.90 A, terminal p.d. = 0.90 x 3.5 = 3.15 V.

questions.topic: Resistivity and conductivity
questions.stem: A length of constantan wire was stretched along a metre rule. Its diameter, measured with a micrometer screw gauge at several points, had a mean value of 0.40 mm. A steady current of 0.50 A, kept constant with a rheostat, was passed through the wire and the p.d. V across a length L was measured with a voltmeter connected by crocodile clips: L/m: 0.20, 0.30, 0.40, 0.50, 0.60, 0.70; V/V: 0.40, 0.57, 0.78, 0.98, 1.16, 1.36. (a)(i) Calculate the resistance R = V/I for each length. [3 marks] (ii) A graph of R (vertical axis) against L gives a best-fit straight line through the origin passing through (0.20 m, 0.78 ohm) and (0.70 m, 2.72 ohm). Determine its slope. [4 marks] (iii) Calculate the cross-sectional area A of the wire. [pi = 3.142] [3 marks] (iv) Using rho = (slope) x A, calculate the resistivity of constantan. [3 marks] (v) Calculate the conductivity of constantan. [2 marks] (vi) State two precautions taken. [2 marks] (b)(i) Define resistivity and state its S.I. unit. [2 marks] (ii) Apart from length, state two factors that affect the resistance of a wire. [2 marks] (iii) A wire has a resistance of 8.0 ohms. Calculate the resistance of a wire of the same material that is twice as long and has half the diameter. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a)(i) R/ohm: 0.80, 1.14, 1.56, 1.96, 2.32, 2.72
4 marks: (a)(ii) slope = (2.72 - 0.78)/(0.70 - 0.20) = 3.88 ohm m^-1
3 marks: (a)(iii) A = pi d^2/4 = 3.142 x (0.40 x 10^-3)^2/4 = 1.257 x 10^-7 m^2
3 marks: (a)(iv) rho = 3.88 x 1.257 x 10^-7 = 4.88 x 10^-7 ohm m (accept 4.6 to 5.2 x 10^-7 ohm m)
2 marks: (a)(v) sigma = 1/rho = 1/(4.88 x 10^-7) = 2.05 x 10^6 ohm^-1 m^-1 (S m^-1)
2 marks: (a)(vi) Any two: current kept small/constant and switched off between readings to avoid heating; diameter measured at several points and averaged; wire kept straight/taut; avoided parallax in reading meters and rule (1 mark each)
2 marks: (b)(i) The resistance of a conductor of unit length and unit cross-sectional area (rho = RA/L) (1 mark); ohm metre (1 mark)
2 marks: (b)(ii) Any two: cross-sectional area (thickness); nature of material (resistivity); temperature (1 mark each)
4 marks: (b)(iii) R is proportional to L/d^2 (1 mark); new R = 8.0 x 2 x (1/(1/2)^2) = 8.0 x 2 x 4 (2 marks) = 64 ohms (1 mark)
questions.explanation: R = V/0.50 = 0.80, 1.14, 1.56, 1.96, 2.32, 2.72 ohm. Slope = (2.72 - 0.78)/(0.70 - 0.20) = 3.88 ohm m^-1 (= R/L). A = pi d^2/4 = 1.257 x 10^-7 m^2, so rho = 3.88 x 1.257 x 10^-7 = 4.88 x 10^-7 ohm m, and conductivity = 1/rho = 2.05 x 10^6 S m^-1. (b) R = rho L/A; doubling L doubles R and halving d quarters A, so R becomes 8.0 x 2 x 4 = 64 ohms.

questions.topic: Measurement of heat energy
questions.stem: An immersion heater connected to a 12.0 V supply drew a steady current of 3.50 A. It was placed in 0.300 kg of water in a well-lagged plastic container of negligible heat capacity. The water was stirred continuously and its temperature theta read every minute: t/min: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6; theta/degrees C: 27.0, 29.1, 30.9, 33.0, 35.1, 36.9, 39.0. (a)(i) Calculate the temperature rise above the initial temperature for each reading. [3 marks] (ii) A graph of theta (vertical axis) against t in seconds gives a best-fit line passing through (0 s, 27.02 degrees C) and (360 s, 38.98 degrees C). Determine its slope. [4 marks] (iii) Calculate the power supplied by the heater. [2 marks] (iv) Assuming no heat is lost, use the relation P = mc x (slope) to calculate the specific heat capacity c of water. [4 marks] (v) Why was the water stirred continuously? [1 mark] (vi) State two precautions taken. [2 marks] (b)(i) Define specific heat capacity. [2 marks] (ii) Distinguish between heat capacity and specific heat capacity. [3 marks] (iii) An electric kettle rated 1500 W contains 2.0 kg of water at 25 degrees C. Calculate the minimum time taken to bring the water to 100 degrees C. [c = 4200 J kg^-1 K^-1] [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a)(i) rise/degrees C: 0.0, 2.1, 3.9, 6.0, 8.1, 9.9, 12.0
4 marks: (a)(ii) slope = (38.98 - 27.02)/(360 - 0) = 0.0332 K s^-1
2 marks: (a)(iii) P = VI = 12.0 x 3.50 = 42.0 W
4 marks: (a)(iv) c = P/(m x slope) = 42.0/(0.300 x 0.0332) = 4210 J kg^-1 K^-1 (accept 4000 to 4400)
1 mark: (a)(v) To distribute the heat evenly so that the thermometer reads the average temperature of the water
2 marks: (a)(vi) Any two: container well lagged; heater fully immersed; thermometer read at eye level; current kept constant with rheostat; thermometer not touching heater (1 mark each)
2 marks: (b)(i) The quantity of heat required to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 K (1 degree C)
3 marks: (b)(ii) Heat capacity is the heat needed to raise the temperature of the whole body by 1 K (unit J K^-1) (1.5 marks); specific heat capacity is per unit mass (unit J kg^-1 K^-1); heat capacity = mass x specific heat capacity (1.5 marks)
4 marks: (b)(iii) Q = mc(theta2 - theta1) = 2.0 x 4200 x 75 = 630 000 J (2 marks); t = Q/P = 630 000/1500 = 420 s (7 minutes) (2 marks)
questions.explanation: Rises: 0.0, 2.1, 3.9, 6.0, 8.1, 9.9, 12.0 degrees C. Slope = (38.98 - 27.02)/360 = 0.0332 K s^-1. P = VI = 42.0 W. Energy per second = mc x rate, so c = 42.0/(0.300 x 0.0332) = 4210 J kg^-1 K^-1 (about 4200). (b) Heat capacity refers to the whole body (J K^-1); specific heat capacity is per kilogram. Kettle: Q = 2.0 x 4200 x 75 = 630 000 J; t = 630 000/1500 = 420 s.

questions.topic: Measurement of heat energy
questions.stem: Pieces of aluminium of total mass m were heated in boiling water at 100.0 degrees C and quickly transferred into 0.100 kg of water at 27.0 degrees C in a lagged plastic cup of negligible heat capacity. The mixture was stirred and the highest steady temperature theta recorded. The experiment was repeated with different masses: m/kg: 0.050, 0.100, 0.150, 0.200, 0.250, 0.300; theta/degrees C: 34.2, 39.8, 44.8, 49.0, 52.4, 55.6. (a)(i) Calculate (theta - 27.0) for each mass. [2 marks] (ii) Calculate (100.0 - theta) for each mass. [2 marks] (iii) Evaluate y = (theta - 27.0)/(100.0 - theta) for each mass, correct to three decimal places. [3 marks] (iv) A graph of y (vertical axis) against m gives a best-fit straight line through the origin passing through (0.05 kg, 0.108) and (0.30 kg, 0.643). Determine its slope s. [4 marks] (v) Given that y = (c/(M cw)) m, where M = 0.100 kg and cw = 4200 J kg^-1 K^-1, calculate the specific heat capacity c of aluminium. [3 marks] (vi) State two precautions taken. [2 marks] (b)(i) Why must the metal be transferred quickly? [2 marks] (ii) State the principle on which the method of mixtures is based. [2 marks] (iii) A 0.50 kg block of copper at 120 degrees C is dropped into 1.0 kg of water at 20 degrees C. Neglecting heat losses, calculate the final temperature. [c(copper) = 400 J kg^-1 K^-1; c(water) = 4200 J kg^-1 K^-1] [5 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a)(i) (theta - 27.0): 7.2, 12.8, 17.8, 22.0, 25.4, 28.6
2 marks: (a)(ii) (100.0 - theta): 65.8, 60.2, 55.2, 51.0, 47.6, 44.4
3 marks: (a)(iii) y: 0.109, 0.213, 0.322, 0.431, 0.534, 0.644
4 marks: (a)(iv) s = (0.643 - 0.108)/(0.30 - 0.05) = 2.140 kg^-1
3 marks: (a)(v) c = s M cw = 2.140 x 0.100 x 4200 = 899 J kg^-1 K^-1 (accept 850 to 950)
2 marks: (a)(vi) Any two: metal transferred quickly; mixture stirred; highest steady temperature recorded; cup lagged/covered; no water splashed out; thermometer read at eye level (1 mark each)
2 marks: (b)(i) To reduce heat lost by the hot metal to the surroundings during transfer
2 marks: (b)(ii) Heat lost by the hot body = heat gained by the cold body (no heat lost to the surroundings)
5 marks: (b)(iii) 0.50 x 400 x (120 - theta) = 1.0 x 4200 x (theta - 20) (2 marks); 24 000 - 200 theta = 4200 theta - 84 000 (1 mark); 4400 theta = 108 000 (1 mark); theta = 24.5 degrees C (1 mark)
questions.explanation: (theta - 27.0) = 7.2, 12.8, 17.8, 22.0, 25.4, 28.6; (100.0 - theta) = 65.8, 60.2, 55.2, 51.0, 47.6, 44.4; y = 0.109, 0.213, 0.322, 0.431, 0.534, 0.644. Heat lost by metal = heat gained by water: m c (100 - theta) = M cw (theta - 27), so y = (c/(M cw)) m. Slope s = 2.140 kg^-1 gives c = 2.140 x 0.100 x 4200 = 899 J kg^-1 K^-1 (aluminium, about 900). (b) Fast transfer limits heat loss; the method relies on heat lost = heat gained. Copper: 200(120 - theta) = 4200(theta - 20), theta = 108 000/4400 = 24.5 degrees C.

questions.topic: Latent heat
questions.stem: In an experiment to determine the specific latent heat of fusion of ice, the following readings were obtained: mass of empty copper calorimeter = 80.0 g; mass of calorimeter + warm water = 280.0 g; initial temperature of water = 40.0 degrees C; small pieces of dried ice at 0 degrees C were added with stirring until the temperature fell to 12.0 degrees C, when all the ice had melted; mass of calorimeter + water + melted ice = 343.2 g. [specific heat capacity of water = 4200 J kg^-1 K^-1; of copper = 400 J kg^-1 K^-1] (a)(i) Calculate the mass of warm water used and the mass of ice added. [3 marks] (ii) Calculate the heat lost by the warm water and the calorimeter. [4 marks] (iii) Calculate the heat gained by the melted ice in warming from 0 degrees C to 12.0 degrees C. [3 marks] (iv) Hence calculate the specific latent heat of fusion of ice. [3 marks] (v) Why was the ice dried before being added? [1 mark] (vi) State two other precautions taken. [2 marks] (b)(i) Define specific latent heat of fusion. [2 marks] (ii) Explain why a scald from steam at 100 degrees C is more severe than one from water at 100 degrees C. [2 marks] (iii) Calculate the heat required to convert 0.20 kg of ice at 0 degrees C to water at 30 degrees C. [specific latent heat of fusion of ice = 3.36 x 10^5 J kg^-1] [5 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a)(i) mass of water = 280.0 - 80.0 = 200.0 g (1.5 marks); mass of ice = 343.2 - 280.0 = 63.2 g (1.5 marks)
4 marks: (a)(ii) heat lost = (0.200 x 4200 + 0.080 x 400)(40.0 - 12.0) = (840 + 32) x 28.0 = 24416 J
3 marks: (a)(iii) heat gained by melted ice = 0.0632 x 4200 x 12.0 = 3185 J
3 marks: (a)(iv) mL = 24416 - 3185 = 21231 J; L = 21231/0.0632 = 3.36 x 10^5 J kg^-1
1 mark: (a)(v) So that no water at 0 degrees C (adhering to the ice) is added, which would be counted as ice and give too low a value
2 marks: (a)(vi) Any two: ice in small pieces; mixture stirred continuously; calorimeter lagged; water started a few degrees above room temperature and finished below it; thermometer read at eye level (1 mark each)
2 marks: (b)(i) The quantity of heat required to change 1 kg of a solid at its melting point into liquid at the same temperature
2 marks: (b)(ii) Steam gives out its large latent heat of vaporisation on condensing on the skin, in addition to the heat given out as the water then cools
5 marks: (b)(iii) melting: 0.20 x 3.36 x 10^5 = 67 200 J (2 marks); warming: 0.20 x 4200 x 30 = 25 200 J (2 marks); total = 92 400 J (1 mark)
questions.explanation: Mass of water = 200.0 g; mass of ice = 63.2 g. Heat lost by water and calorimeter = (0.200 x 4200 + 0.080 x 400) x 28.0 = 24416 J. Heat gained by melted ice warming to 12.0 degrees C = 0.0632 x 4200 x 12.0 = 3185 J. Heat used to melt the ice = 21231 J, so L = 21231/0.0632 = 3.36 x 10^5 J kg^-1 (accepted value 3.36 x 10^5). (b) Steam releases latent heat on condensing, so it burns more. Ice: 67 200 + 25 200 = 92 400 J.

questions.topic: Thermal expansion
questions.stem: A brass rod of length 0.600 m at 30 degrees C was placed in a steam jacket with one end against a fixed stop and the other end touching the plunger of a dial gauge. Water at different temperatures theta was circulated through the jacket and the increase in length x of the rod was read from the gauge: theta/degrees C: 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80, 90; x/mm: 0.00, 0.12, 0.22, 0.34, 0.47, 0.56, 0.68. (a)(i) Calculate the temperature rise (theta - 30) for each reading. [2 marks] (ii) Express each value of x in metres. [2 marks] (iii) A graph of x in mm (vertical axis) against theta gives a best-fit straight line passing through (30 degrees C, 0.002 mm) and (90 degrees C, 0.681 mm). Determine its slope in m K^-1. [4 marks] (iv) Calculate the linear expansivity of brass. [3 marks] (v) State the unit of linear expansivity. [1 mark] (vi) State two precautions taken. [2 marks] (vii) Why was the rod made long? [2 marks] (b)(i) Define linear expansivity. [2 marks] (ii) A steel rail is 20 m long. Calculate the gap that must be left between rails to allow for a temperature rise of 30 K. [linear expansivity of steel = 1.2 x 10^-5 K^-1] [3 marks] (iii) State two applications of the bimetallic strip. [2 marks] (iv) State two problems caused by thermal expansion in everyday life. [2 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a)(i) (theta - 30)/K: 0, 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60
2 marks: (a)(ii) x/m: 0.00000, 0.00012, 0.00022, 0.00034, 0.00047, 0.00056, 0.00068
4 marks: (a)(iii) slope = (0.681 - 0.002)/(90 - 30) = 0.01132 mm K^-1 = 1.132 x 10^-5 m K^-1
3 marks: (a)(iv) alpha = slope/L0 = 1.132 x 10^-5/0.600 = 1.89 x 10^-5 K^-1 (accept 1.8 to 2.0 x 10^-5 K^-1)
1 mark: (a)(v) per kelvin (K^-1)
2 marks: (a)(vi) Any two: waited for the temperature to become steady before reading; gauge read without parallax; dial gauge zeroed at start; rod firmly against the stop; thermometer in the jacket near the rod (1 mark each)
2 marks: (a)(vii) The expansion is very small; a long rod gives a larger, more measurable extension and a smaller percentage error
2 marks: (b)(i) The increase in length per unit original length per degree (kelvin) rise in temperature
3 marks: (b)(ii) gap = alpha L theta = 1.2 x 10^-5 x 20 x 30 = 7.2 x 10^-3 m = 7.2 mm
2 marks: (b)(iii) Any two: thermostat (pressing iron, fridge, oven); fire alarm; bimetallic thermometer; flashing indicator/circuit breaker (1 mark each)
2 marks: (b)(iv) Any two: buckling of rails; cracking of thick glass with hot water; sagging/snapping of overhead cables; bursting of tightly-filled containers; cracking of concrete roads/bridges (1 mark each)

questions.topic: Principle of moments
questions.stem: A uniform metre rule was balanced horizontally on a knife-edge at the 50.0 cm mark. An object X of unknown mass was suspended at the 20.0 cm mark. Known masses m were suspended in turn on the other side of the knife-edge and moved until the rule balanced horizontally; the position P of each known mass was read: m/g: 40, 50, 60, 70, 80, 90, 100; P/cm: 95.1, 85.9, 80.0, 75.8, 72.4, 70.1, 68.0. (a)(i) Calculate the distance d = P - 50.0 cm of each known mass from the knife-edge. [3 marks] (ii) Calculate 1/m (in g^-1) for each mass, correct to four decimal places. [3 marks] (iii) A graph of d (vertical axis) against 1/m is a straight line through the origin passing through (0.010 g^-1, 18.0 cm) and (0.025 g^-1, 45.0 cm). Determine its slope. [4 marks] (iv) Use the principle of moments to show that the slope equals 30 X, and hence find the mass of X. [3 marks] (v) State two precautions taken. [2 marks] (b)(i) State the principle of moments. [2 marks] (ii) State the two conditions for a rigid body to be in equilibrium under parallel forces. [2 marks] (iii) A uniform metre rule of mass 100 g is pivoted at the 30 cm mark. Calculate the mass that must be hung at the 5 cm mark to keep it horizontal. [4 marks] (iv) What is a couple? [2 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a)(i) d/cm: 45.1, 35.9, 30.0, 25.8, 22.4, 20.1, 18.0
3 marks: (a)(ii) 1/m: 0.0250, 0.0200, 0.0167, 0.0143, 0.0125, 0.0111, 0.0100 g^-1
4 marks: (a)(iii) slope = (45.0 - 18.0)/(0.025 - 0.010) = 1800 g cm
3 marks: (a)(iv) X x 30 = m d, so d = 30X (1/m) and slope = 30X (1 mark); X = 1800/30 = 60.0 g (2 marks) (accept 58 to 62 g)
2 marks: (a)(v) Any two: rule balanced horizontally before loading; threads of masses kept vertical/thin; rule allowed to come to rest; positions read without parallax; no draughts (1 mark each)
2 marks: (b)(i) When a body is in equilibrium, the sum of the clockwise moments about any point equals the sum of the anticlockwise moments about the same point
2 marks: (b)(ii) The sum of upward forces equals the sum of downward forces (resultant force zero); the sum of clockwise moments equals the sum of anticlockwise moments about any point
4 marks: (b)(iii) weight of rule acts at 50 cm, 20 cm from pivot; mass m at 25 cm from pivot (1 mark); m x 25 = 100 x 20 (2 marks); m = 80 g (1 mark)
2 marks: (b)(iv) Two equal, parallel and opposite forces whose lines of action do not coincide; they produce rotation only
questions.explanation: d = P - 50.0 = 45.1, 35.9, 30.0, 25.8, 22.4, 20.1, 18.0 cm; 1/m = 0.0250, 0.0200, 0.0167, 0.0143, 0.0125, 0.0111, 0.0100 g^-1. Slope = 1800 g cm. Taking moments about the knife-edge: X x 30 = m d, so d = 30X(1/m), slope = 30X and X = 1800/30 = 60.0 g. (b) Principle of moments: sum of clockwise moments = sum of anticlockwise moments in equilibrium. Rule: 100 x 20 = m x 25, m = 80 g. A couple is two equal antiparallel forces not in line.

questions.topic: Conditions for equilibrium of rigid bodies
questions.stem: The centre of gravity of a uniform metre rule was found to be at the 50.0 cm mark. A mass m was hung at the 5.0 cm mark and the rule was balanced horizontally on a knife-edge, whose position P was read. The procedure was repeated with different masses: m/g: 20, 40, 60, 80, 100; P/cm: 43.7, 38.7, 35.1, 32.0, 29.4. (a)(i) Calculate a = (P - 5.0) cm for each reading. [2 marks] (ii) Calculate b = (50.0 - P) cm for each reading. [2 marks] (iii) Evaluate y = b/a for each reading, correct to three decimal places. [3 marks] (iv) A graph of y (vertical axis) against m gives a best-fit straight line through the origin passing through (20 g, 0.162) and (100 g, 0.840). Determine its slope s. [4 marks] (v) Show that s = 1/M, where M is the mass of the rule, and hence find M. [3 marks] (vi) State two precautions taken. [2 marks] (b)(i) Define centre of gravity. [2 marks] (ii) Distinguish between stable, unstable and neutral equilibrium, giving an example of each. [3 marks] (iii) State two ways of increasing the stability of a body. [2 marks] (iv) Explain why racing cars are built low and wide. [2 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: (a)(i) a/cm: 38.7, 33.7, 30.1, 27.0, 24.4
2 marks: (a)(ii) b/cm: 6.3, 11.3, 14.9, 18.0, 20.6
3 marks: (a)(iii) y: 0.163, 0.335, 0.495, 0.667, 0.844
4 marks: (a)(iv) s = (0.840 - 0.162)/(100 - 20) = 0.00848 g^-1
3 marks: (a)(v) moments about knife-edge: m a = M b, so b/a = m/M and slope = 1/M (1 mark); M = 1/0.00848 = 118 g (2 marks) (accept 110 to 130 g)
2 marks: (a)(vi) Any two: rule balanced horizontally each time; mass hung with thin thread exactly at the 5.0 cm mark; knife-edge position read without parallax; draughts avoided (1 mark each)
2 marks: (b)(i) The point through which the resultant weight of a body acts
3 marks: (b)(ii) Stable: returns to original position when slightly displaced (cone on its base); unstable: moves further away (cone on its apex); neutral: stays in new position (cone on its side/ball on a table) (1 mark each)
2 marks: (b)(iii) Lower the centre of gravity; widen the base (1 mark each)
2 marks: (b)(iv) A low centre of gravity and wide base mean the car can tilt through a large angle before its weight acts outside the base, so it does not overturn easily at bends
questions.explanation: a = 38.7, 33.7, 30.1, 27.0, 24.4 cm; b = 6.3, 11.3, 14.9, 18.0, 20.6 cm; y = b/a = 0.163, 0.335, 0.495, 0.667, 0.844. Taking moments about the knife-edge: m(P - 5) = M(50 - P), so y = m/M. Slope s = 0.00848 g^-1, M = 1/s = 118 g. (b) The centre of gravity is where the whole weight appears to act; stability is increased by a low centre of gravity and wide base.

questions.topic: Law of flotation
questions.stem: A flat-bottomed test tube of uniform cross-section was floated upright in water (density 1.00 g cm^-3) in a measuring cylinder. Lead shots of total mass m were added and the depth h of the tube below the water surface was measured with a strip of graph paper inside the tube: m/g: 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60; h/cm: 7.6, 9.9, 12.5, 15.1, 17.4, 20.0. (a)(i) A graph of h (vertical axis) against m gives a best-fit straight line passing through (10 g, 7.53 cm) and (60 g, 19.97 cm). Determine its slope s and its intercept c on the h axis. [6 marks] (ii) Given that h = (m + M)/(rho A), where M is the mass of the empty tube, rho the density of water and A the cross-sectional area of the tube, use s to find A. [3 marks] (iii) Use c and A to find M. [3 marks] (iv) Why were lead shots used to load the tube? [1 mark] (v) State two precautions taken. [2 marks] (b)(i) State the law of flotation. [2 marks] (ii) State Archimedes' principle. [2 marks] (iii) A block of wood of density 0.60 g cm^-3 floats in water. What fraction of its volume is submerged? [2 marks] (iv) A metal object weighs 5.0 N in air, 3.0 N when fully immersed in water and 3.4 N when fully immersed in a liquid L. Calculate the relative density of the metal and of L. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
6 marks: (a)(i) s = (19.97 - 7.53)/(60 - 10) = 0.249 cm g^-1 (4 marks); c = 7.53 - 0.249 x 10 = 5.04 cm (2 marks)
3 marks: (a)(ii) s = 1/(rho A), so A = 1/(1.00 x 0.249) = 4.0 cm^2 (accept 3.8 to 4.2 cm^2)
3 marks: (a)(iii) c = M/(rho A), so M = c rho A = 5.04 x 1.00 x 4.0 = 20.2 g (accept 18 to 22 g)
1 mark: (a)(iv) To lower the centre of gravity so that the tube floats upright (and to vary the load in small steps)
2 marks: (a)(v) Any two: tube floated freely without touching the sides of the cylinder; depth read at eye level/avoided parallax; tube kept dry inside; shots spread evenly at the bottom (1 mark each)
2 marks: (b)(i) A floating body displaces its own weight of the fluid in which it floats
2 marks: (b)(ii) When a body is wholly or partially immersed in a fluid, it experiences an upthrust equal to the weight of the fluid displaced
2 marks: (b)(iii) fraction submerged = density of wood/density of water = 0.60/1.00 = 0.60 (three-fifths)
4 marks: (b)(iv) upthrust in water = 2.0 N; R.D. of metal = 5.0/2.0 = 2.5 (2 marks); upthrust in L = 1.6 N; R.D. of L = 1.6/2.0 = 0.80 (2 marks)
questions.explanation: Slope s = (19.97 - 7.53)/(50) = 0.249 cm g^-1; intercept c = 5.04 cm. By the law of flotation, weight of tube + shots = weight of water displaced: (m + M) = rho A h, so s = 1/(rho A), giving A = 4.0 cm^2, and c = M/(rho A), giving M = 20.2 g. (b) Wood of density 0.60 g cm^-3 floats with 0.60 of its volume submerged. Metal: R.D. = 5.0/(5.0 - 3.0) = 2.5; liquid: R.D. = (5.0 - 3.4)/(5.0 - 3.0) = 0.80.

questions.topic: Vibration of air in pipes: open and closed pipes
questions.stem: A resonance tube, open at the top, was clamped vertically in a tall jar of water so that the length of the air column could be varied. A sounding tuning fork of frequency f was held over the open end and the tube raised slowly from the water until the first loud sound (first resonance) was heard. The length l of the air column was measured. This was repeated with other forks: f/Hz: 256, 288, 320, 384, 480, 512; l/cm: 31.7, 27.8, 25.0, 20.6, 16.0, 15.1. (a)(i) Calculate 1/f for each fork, correct to five decimal places. [3 marks] (ii) A graph of l (vertical axis) against 1/f gives a best-fit straight line passing through (0.002 s, 15.44 cm) and (0.004 s, 32.39 cm). Determine its slope and its intercept on the l axis. [4 marks] (iii) Given that l + e = v/(4f), where e is the end correction, use the slope to find the speed of sound v in air in m s^-1. [4 marks] (iv) Use the intercept to find e. [2 marks] (v) How was the first resonance recognised? [2 marks] (vi) State two precautions taken. [2 marks] (b)(i) State two differences between a stationary wave and a progressive wave. [2 marks] (ii) A pipe closed at one end is 0.85 m long. Neglecting end correction, calculate the frequency of its fundamental note and of its first overtone. [speed of sound in air = 340 m s^-1] [4 marks] (iii) Explain the term resonance. [2 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a)(i) 1/f in s: 0.00391, 0.00347, 0.00313, 0.00260, 0.00208, 0.00195
4 marks: (a)(ii) slope = (32.39 - 15.44)/(0.004 - 0.002) = 8475 cm s^-1 (2 marks); intercept = -1.51 cm (2 marks)
4 marks: (a)(iii) slope = v/4, so v = 4 x 8475 cm s^-1 = 339 m s^-1 (accept 330 to 350 m s^-1)
2 marks: (a)(iv) intercept = -e, so e = 1.5 cm
2 marks: (a)(v) The sound from the tube became loudest (the air column vibrated with maximum amplitude, in step with the fork)
2 marks: (a)(vi) Any two: fork held horizontally just above the open end without touching the tube; tube raised slowly from the lowest position to find the FIRST resonance; length read at eye level/avoided parallax; tube vertical; noisy surroundings avoided (1 mark each)
2 marks: (b)(i) Any two: a stationary wave has nodes and antinodes, a progressive wave does not; a stationary wave does not transfer energy along the medium, a progressive wave does; amplitude varies from point to point in a stationary wave but is the same for all points of a progressive wave; particles between adjacent nodes vibrate in phase in a stationary wave (1 mark each)
4 marks: (b)(ii) fundamental f0 = v/(4L) = 340/(4 x 0.85) = 100 Hz (2 marks); first overtone = 3f0 = 300 Hz (2 marks)
2 marks: (b)(iii) Resonance occurs when a body is set into vibration at its natural frequency by another vibrating body of the same frequency, giving vibrations of maximum amplitude
questions.explanation: 1/f = 0.00391, 0.00347, 0.00313, 0.00260, 0.00208, 0.00195 s. Slope = (32.39 - 15.44)/(0.002) = 8475 cm s^-1 and intercept = -1.51 cm. Since l = (v/4)(1/f) - e, v = 4 x slope = 339 m s^-1 and e = 1.5 cm. (b) A closed pipe of 0.85 m gives f0 = 340/3.4 = 100 Hz; its first overtone is the third harmonic, 300 Hz.

questions.topic: Vibration in strings
questions.stem: A sonometer wire was kept under a constant tension of 40 N. A sounding tuning fork was placed with its stem on the sonometer box and the length of wire between the bridges was adjusted until a small paper rider placed at the middle of the wire was thrown off. The vibrating length l was recorded for each fork of frequency f: f/Hz: 256, 288, 320, 384, 426.7, 512; l/cm: 39.3, 34.6, 31.4, 25.9, 23.5, 19.4. (a)(i) Calculate 1/l in m^-1 for each length, correct to three decimal places. [3 marks] (ii) A graph of f (vertical axis) against 1/l gives a best-fit straight line through the origin passing through (2.5 m^-1, 251 Hz) and (5.0 m^-1, 498 Hz). Determine its slope. [4 marks] (iii) Given that f = (1/(2l)) sqrt(T/mu), the slope equals v/2, where v is the speed of transverse waves on the wire. Find v. [3 marks] (iv) Use v = sqrt(T/mu) to calculate the mass per unit length mu of the wire. [3 marks] (v) Using your slope, predict the frequency of the note given by 0.25 m of the wire under the same tension. [2 marks] (vi) State two precautions taken. [2 marks] (b)(i) State the three laws of vibration of stretched strings. [3 marks] (ii) What is the purpose of the paper rider? [2 marks] (iii) A string of length 0.50 m vibrates in its fundamental mode at 200 Hz. Calculate the speed of the waves on it, and the new fundamental frequency if the tension is made four times as large. [3 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a)(i) 1/l/m^-1: 2.545, 2.890, 3.185, 3.861, 4.255, 5.155
4 marks: (a)(ii) slope = (498 - 251)/(5.0 - 2.5) = 98.8 m s^-1 (Hz m)
3 marks: (a)(iii) v = 2 x slope = 198 m s^-1 (accept 190 to 210 m s^-1)
3 marks: (a)(iv) mu = T/v^2 = 40/198^2 = 1.02 x 10^-3 kg m^-1
2 marks: (a)(v) f = slope x (1/0.25) = 98.8 x 4.0 = 395 Hz
2 marks: (a)(vi) Any two: rider placed exactly at the middle of the vibrating length; fork struck on a rubber pad, not on a hard surface; tension kept constant; bridge distances read without parallax (1 mark each)
3 marks: (b)(i) For a stretched string: f is inversely proportional to its length (T and mu constant); f is proportional to the square root of the tension (l and mu constant); f is inversely proportional to the square root of the mass per unit length (l and T constant) (1 mark each)
2 marks: (b)(ii) It shows when resonance occurs: the wire vibrates with maximum amplitude at the natural frequency matching the fork and throws off the rider
3 marks: (b)(iii) lambda = 2l = 1.0 m, v = f lambda = 200 m s^-1 (1.5 marks); f is proportional to sqrt(T), so new f = 200 x sqrt(4) = 400 Hz (1.5 marks)
questions.explanation: 1/l = 2.545, 2.890, 3.185, 3.861, 4.255, 5.155 m^-1. Slope = (498 - 251)/(2.5) = 98.8 m s^-1, so v = 2 x slope = 198 m s^-1 and mu = T/v^2 = 1.02 x 10^-3 kg m^-1. For 0.25 m, f = 98.8 x 4 = 395 Hz. (b) In the fundamental mode lambda = 2l = 1.0 m so v = 200 m s^-1; quadrupling T doubles f to 400 Hz.

questions.topic: The gas laws
questions.stem: Dry air was trapped in a uniform glass tube by a column of mercury. The pressure P on the air was changed using a mercury reservoir and the length L of the trapped air column was measured each time at constant room temperature: P/cmHg: 66, 76, 86, 96, 106, 116; L/cm: 28.9, 25.0, 22.0, 19.9, 17.8, 16.5. (a)(i) Calculate 1/L (in cm^-1) for each reading, correct to four decimal places. [3 marks] (ii) Calculate the product PL for each reading. [3 marks] (iii) A graph of P (vertical axis) against 1/L gives a best-fit straight line through the origin passing through (0.035 cm^-1, 66.5 cmHg) and (0.060 cm^-1, 114.1 cmHg). Determine its slope. [4 marks] (iv) What do your results in (ii) and (iii) show about the relationship between pressure and volume of the trapped air? [2 marks] (v) Why was it necessary to wait a short time after each change of pressure before taking a reading? [2 marks] (vi) State two precautions taken. [2 marks] (b)(i) State Boyle's law. [2 marks] (ii) Use the kinetic theory to explain why the pressure of a fixed mass of gas increases when its volume is reduced at constant temperature. [3 marks] (iii) A fixed mass of gas occupies 2.0 dm^3 at 300 K and 1.0 x 10^5 Pa. Calculate its volume at 400 K and 1.5 x 10^5 Pa. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: (a)(i) 1/L/cm^-1: 0.0346, 0.0400, 0.0455, 0.0503, 0.0562, 0.0606
3 marks: (a)(ii) PL/cmHg cm: 1907, 1900, 1892, 1910, 1887, 1914
4 marks: (a)(iii) slope = (114.1 - 66.5)/(0.060 - 0.035) = 1904 cmHg cm
2 marks: (a)(iv) PL is constant (about equal to the slope) and P is proportional to 1/L; since V is proportional to L for a uniform tube, PV = constant: pressure is inversely proportional to volume (Boyle's law)
2 marks: (a)(v) To allow the air to return to room temperature (compression warms it slightly), so that the temperature is constant
2 marks: (a)(vi) Any two: tube kept vertical; mercury levels and lengths read at eye level/no parallax; temperature kept constant; air kept dry; changes made slowly (1 mark each)
2 marks: (b)(i) The volume of a fixed mass of gas is inversely proportional to its pressure, provided the temperature is constant
3 marks: (b)(ii) At constant temperature the molecules have the same average speed; reducing the volume increases the number of molecules per unit volume (1.5 marks); so they collide with the walls more frequently, giving a greater force per unit area, i.e. higher pressure (1.5 marks)
4 marks: (b)(iii) P1V1/T1 = P2V2/T2 (1 mark); V2 = (1.0 x 10^5 x 2.0 x 400)/(300 x 1.5 x 10^5) (2 marks) = 1.78 dm^3 (1 mark)
